Hook: In 2001 and 2002, two economists, Marianne Bertrand and Sendhil Mullainathan, answered help-wanted advertisements in Boston and Chicago newspapers with invented résumés. Some were headed Emily or Greg, others Lakisha or Jamal: names chosen because they sound White or African American. Apart from the name, the résumés were alike, and which name went on which résumé was decided at random. In all they sent 4,870 résumés to 1,323 advertisements, and waited for the telephone.

Here is every résumé, one square each. Of the résumés with White-sounding names, 235 were called back, 9.7 percent, about one in ten. Of those with African-American-sounding names, 157, 6.4 percent, about one in fifteen. The same résumés, with names randomly assigned: White names received 50 percent more call-backs, a difference far too large to be chance.

That is one gap, measured cleanly. This part asks the larger question: why are some people paid so much more than others, and how much of the gap is unfair? Why did the reward for a college degree rise, and why has it stalled? What did computers and robots do to the jobs in the middle? How much of a person's pay is their employer, their union, the risks of their job? And what is discrimination, and how can anyone measure it?
Economics, Built. Part thirty-nine: the wage structure.

Here is the plan. How the wage distribution has moved since 1979, and the race between education and technology. A game, and then tasks, polarization and robots. Firms, superstars and unions, and the price of a job's risks. Discrimination, in theory and measured, and the gender gap. Three dials, pay audits, and the frontier.
Wages: Chapter one. The wage distribution since 1979.

Start with the simplest measure of how education is paid. In 1979 the median full-time worker with a college degree earned 1.38 times as much each week as the median high-school graduate. By 1992 the ratio was 1.73: most of the rise came in a single decade, the 1980s. Since then it has crept up, to 1.80 in 2025, and has hardly moved for fifteen years. Below it, the gap between high-school graduates and those who never finished widened too. Whatever happened, it rewarded schooling, and it happened fastest in the 1980s.

What about the typical worker? The median full-time worker's weekly pay, in dollars of 1982 to 1984, was 332 in 1979 and 374 in 2025: 13 percent more in forty-six years, while output per hour worked in the business sector grew 2.4 times. The spread can be read from the deciles, published since 2000. A worker at the ninetieth percentile earned 4.5 times as much as one at the tenth in 2000, and 4.7 times in 2025. All of that widening is at the top: the ninetieth percentile pulled away from the median, while the median moved closer to the tenth, as many states raised their minimum wages and low-wage labour markets tightened after 2020.

A sharper picture ranks occupations, not people. David Autor and David Dorn sorted every occupation by its mean wage in 1980, from the lowest paid to the highest, and asked how each one's wages grew to 2005. Each grey dot is a percentile of 1980 employment; the line smooths them. Wages at the bottom grew by about 0.16 in logs, at the top by 0.26, and in the middle by only 0.12. Growth was not a ramp rising with skill but a U: the middle was hollowed out. The rest of this part tries to explain both shapes.
Race: Chapter two. The race between education and technology.

The simplest explanation is a market for skill with two goods: college and high-school labour. In the 1970s Jan Tinbergen called it a race. Firms combine the two kinds of worker with an elasticity of substitution sigma; technology changes how productive each is. The college premium then depends on two things: relative demand, pushed up by technology, and relative supply, pushed up by schooling. Supply is set by how many people finish college: here it is, in 1992, and demand slopes down, with slope minus one over sigma. By 2025, college graduates had become far more plentiful relative to high-school graduates, and yet the premium rose. With supply moving that far right, only a rightward shift in demand can explain it: technology must have raised the demand for skill.

To measure sigma, Lawrence Katz and Kevin Murphy in 1992 regressed the premium on a time trend, standing for steady growth in demand, and on relative supply. Over 1963 to 1987 the coefficient on supply was about minus 0.71, an elasticity of substitution of 1.41. Try the same regression on the years since 1992. Relative supply has grown almost exactly in a straight line, so it is nearly identical to the time trend: their correlation is 0.997. The regression cannot tell them apart, and returns a negative elasticity, which makes no sense. Katz and Murphy had an advantage: supply growth slowed sharply in the 1980s, breaking the link with the trend. A model is identified only by the variation the data happen to contain.

So fix sigma from earlier work and ask the model a different question: how fast must demand have grown to produce the premium we see, given the supply we see? With sigma at 1.41, relative demand for college workers grew 2.4 percent a year in the 1990s, 2.2 in the 2000s, and 1.7 since 2010. With the larger elasticities that other designs find, between one and a half and two and a half, the numbers are smaller but the shape is the same. Meanwhile supply grew 2.7 percent a year, which at sigma 1.41 pulls the premium down by 1.9 percent a year. Demand outran it in the 1990s; since 2010 it has fallen just behind, and the premium has edged down. Claudia Goldin and Lawrence Katz call this the race between education and technology: in the 1980s technology ran far ahead and the premium soared; lately education has kept pace. Autor, Goldin and Katz find that rising returns to education explain three-quarters of the rise in wage inequality from 1980 to 2000 but well under half since: something else is now at work.
PlayIt: Chapter three. Play it: what happened to twelve kinds of work.

Your turn. Here are twelve kinds of work, from managers to machine operators, from health aides to clerks. Between 1980 and 2005, computers spread through American offices and factories. Which of these grew as a share of all jobs, and which shrank? Sort them in your head into growers and shrinkers, and guess which shrank most. Pause, and choose.

Here is what happened. The biggest loser: machine operators and assemblers, whose share of jobs fell by 54 percent. Skilled production crafts fell 38 percent; clerical work and driving fell too. The growers sit at both ends of the pay scale: professionals, managers and financial sales at the top, and at the bottom child care, health aides, food service and cleaning. 5 of the twelve shrank, and they share one thing: in 1980 they paid middling wages, for work that followed rules.

Plot the same twelve against their pay in 1980. The losses cluster in the middle of the pay scale; gains are at the low end and the high end. Now colour each by how routine its tasks were, a measure built from the government's job descriptions: how much of the work follows explicit rules a machine could be programmed to follow. The most routine work, clerical jobs and machine operating, shrank most. But routineness is a tendency, not a law: food service counts as fairly routine and still grew, and driving counts as hardly routine and still shrank. The next chapter builds the idea properly.
Tasks: In 2003 David Autor, Frank Levy and Richard Murnane proposed looking not at workers' skills but at the tasks a job is made of. Routine cognitive tasks, like bookkeeping or checking a claim, follow explicit rules, and a computer can be programmed to follow them: it substitutes for the worker. Routine manual tasks, assembling or sorting, likewise. Non-routine analytic and interactive tasks, research, management, persuasion, are hard to write down, and the computer makes the people who do them more productive: it complements them. And non-routine manual tasks, cleaning, cooking, caring for someone, need eyes and hands in an unpredictable world, and computers have hardly touched them. Routine tasks were concentrated in middle-paid jobs: the factory floor and the back office.

Now count jobs instead of wages. Rank occupations by their 1980 wage, as before, and ask how each percentile's share of employment changed to 2005: each grey dot is one percentile. Smoothed, the curve is a U again: employment grew at the bottom and at the top, and shrank between the fifteenth and the fiftieth percentiles. In the 1980s alone, the bottom had barely grown: the U came later, as low-paid service jobs expanded. Underneath, the share of each percentile's jobs that were routine in 1980. The routine jobs were piled in the lower middle, exactly where employment fell. This is polarization: the labour market emptied in the middle and filled at both ends.

Daron Acemoglu and David Autor turned this into a model, which Agora solves. Line up every task in the economy, from simplest to most complex. Three kinds of worker share them out: each is relatively better at more complex tasks the more skilled they are, so low-skill workers take the simple end, high-skill workers the complex end, and the middle takes the middle. The boundaries settle where an employer is indifferent between the two neighbouring kinds of worker. Now let machines take over a band of middle tasks, a fifth of the line. Displaced middle-skill workers move down the line, into simpler tasks that low-skill workers used to do, and push them into fewer tasks still; high-skill workers keep the complex end. The middle's wage falls relative to both neighbours': the middle-to-low ratio falls from 1.26 to 1.20, and the high-to-middle ratio rises from 1.68 to 1.82. Technology that replaces tasks, not skills, hollows out the middle and can push its workers down the ladder.
Robots: Computers replaced routine office tasks; industrial robots replace routine tasks on the factory floor: welding, painting, assembling. Daron Acemoglu and Pascual Restrepo asked what they did to American towns. Industries adopt robots at very different rates; carmakers most of all. Towns differ in their mix of industries, so each town's exposure is its industries' adoption rates, weighted by how many of its people worked in each. Then compare towns, really commuting zones, by exposure: did the more exposed lose more jobs, and see slower wage growth? It is the same shift-share logic as the China shock in Part thirty-six. On the Island, six industries adopt robots at these rates.

Run the design on the Island's three hundred commuting zones, where the truth is planted: each robot per thousand workers lowers the employment rate by 0.2 of a percentage point. Each dot is a zone. The simple slope says minus 0.68, more than three times the truth. Why? The zones with the most robots are manufacturing towns, and manufacturing was shrinking anyway, from trade and offshoring. Hold the manufacturing share fixed and the estimate falls to minus 0.27, with a standard error of 0.04: the planted minus 0.2 lies inside its interval. Acemoglu and Restrepo spend much of their paper on exactly this: separating robots from everything else hitting the same towns.

What did they find in America? One more robot per thousand workers lowered a zone's employment-to-population ratio by 0.2 percentage points, and its wages by 0.42 percent. The effects are distinct from imports from China and Mexico, offshoring, other information technology and the decline of routine jobs, and the most exposed zones showed no different trends before the robots came. Robots are still few, so their total effect so far is modest; but they show that some technology simply replaces workers, rather than making them more productive. The open question is artificial intelligence, which can do some non-routine tasks as well. Part sixty-five takes it up.
Firms: Chapter six. Firms: the same worker, a different wage.

Some employers pay more than others for the same work. To measure it, John Abowd, Francis Kramarz and David Margolis wrote each wage as the sum of two parts. A worker effect, alpha, which travels with the person, and a firm effect, psi, a premium the firm pays whoever works there. Here is one islander's log wage over six years. They change firms, and their wage jumps by the difference between the two firms' premiums, from +0.45 to -0.26. Workers who move are what separate firm effects from worker effects: the same person, in two places. With millions of workers in administrative records, the model can be fitted to an entire country.

With the model fitted, the variance of log wages splits into parts. On the Island, where the truth is planted, worker effects account for 67 percent of it, firm effects for 11 percent, and sorting, the tendency of good workers to work at high-paying firms, for 16. The estimates, from six years of a twenty-thousand-worker panel, land close. David Card, Jörg Heining and Patrick Kline fitted the model to West Germany's social security records. Between the late 1980s and the 2000s the firm effects' share rose from 18.5 to 21.2 percent, and sorting's from 2.3 to 16.4 percent. Of the whole rise in German wage inequality, about a quarter came from wider gaps between firms and a third from better workers concentrating in better-paying firms.

But the method has a trap, and the Island can show it. Rerun the economy with fewer and fewer workers changing firms each year. With few movers, each firm's premium is estimated from a handful of people, and their noise looks like real differences between firms: the estimated variance of firm effects doubles when only half a percent move. Worse, the same noise enters a worker's effect with the opposite sign, so the correlation between good workers and good firms is pushed down, and can even turn negative, though the true correlation never changes. This limited-mobility bias made early studies find little sorting. Recent corrections, such as Kline, Saggio and Sølvsten's leave-out estimator, generally shrink the firm effects and raise the sorting.
Stars: Chapter seven. Superstars and the labour share.

In 1981 Sherwin Rosen asked why the best performers in some trades earn so much more than the merely good, when their talents differ so little. His answer was reach. On the Island, talent varies only a little: the most talented one percent hold 1.3 percent of all talent. If a performer can only serve a room, earnings track talent, the grey line. When a recording or a broadcast lets one performer serve a whole country, audiences flock to the best, and earnings become a steep function of talent. Steeper still, and a tiny edge in talent becomes a vast difference in pay: with the steepest curve, the top one percent take 6.3 percent of earnings, and the ninety-ninth percentile earns 6.4 times the median. Technology that widens reach stretches the top of the distribution, for singers, surgeons, chief executives and software.

Superstars can be firms as well as people. Here is the share of income in America's business sector that goes to labour, as an index. It was steady for decades; since 1980 it has fallen by about 14 percent. In 2020 David Autor, David Dorn, Lawrence Katz, Christina Patterson and John Van Reenen looked inside, firm by firm. The typical firm's labour share barely fell. What changed is that sales and value added moved towards a few superstar firms, which are highly productive and pay a small share of their revenue to labour. The industries where concentration rose most saw the largest falls in the labour share. A winner-take-most economy shifts income from wages to profits, and within wages, towards those who work at the winners.
Unions: Unions bargain for a whole workplace at once, and they have been shrinking. In 1983, the first year of comparable figures, 20.1 percent of American employees belonged to a union. By 2024, 9.9 percent. What remains is mostly in government, where 32.2 percent belong; in private firms, 5.9 percent. What did their decline do to the wage structure?

First, the premium. Here are 545 young American men followed from 1980 to 1987, about a quarter of them in a union in any year. Union members earned about 20 percent more. Controlling for schooling, experience, marriage and race leaves the gap at 0.18 log points. But union jobs may go to different kinds of men. So compare each man with himself, in the years he was in a union and the years he was not. The premium falls to 0.08, with a standard error of 0.02: still about eight percent, but less than half the cross-sectional gap. Much of the raw gap was who joins, not what the union does.

Unions also change the shape of pay. In a 1985 sample from the Current Population Survey, the log wages of non-union workers spread widely, while union members' are bunched together: a standard deviation of 0.42 against 0.53. Contracts set standard rates for jobs and seniority scales, and narrow the gaps by schooling and skill. In these data the union premium was about 0.20 log points in both 1978 and 1985, while the union share of the sample fell from 31 to 18 percent. With fewer workers covered, less of the labour market is compressed: studies attribute a real part of the rise in men's wage inequality since the 1970s to the decline of unions.
Hedonic: Not every pay gap is a puzzle. Adam Smith noticed in 1776 that wages vary with the ease or hardship, the cleanliness or dirtiness, the honour or dishonour of the work. If a job is dangerous or unpleasant, an employer must pay more to fill it with the same kind of worker. Such a gap is not unfair; it is a price, the compensating differential for the job's drawbacks.

In 1974 Sherwin Rosen showed what such a price means in a market. On the Island, workers differ in how much they mind risk, and firms differ in how costly it is to make their work safe. Workers who mind risk least end up in the firms where safety is dearest, and take the riskiest jobs, at higher pay. The jobs trace out a wage locus. At each job, the locus is tangent to the indifference line of the worker who holds it: its slope is exactly what that worker needs to accept a little more risk. So a regression of wages on risk measures a price, about 1.10 here, close to the islanders' average distaste of 1.09. The same logic, applied to the risk of death at work, gives the value of a statistical life that governments use to weigh safety rules. But it reads the preferences of those who sorted into risky jobs, who mind risk least.

Hours are a job characteristic too. In 2017 Alexandre Mas and Amanda Pallais ran an experiment inside a real hiring process: applicants to a national call centre were offered jobs with different schedules at different wages. The average applicant would give up 20 percent of wages to avoid a schedule an employer sets at short notice, and 8 percent for the option of working from home. Most would pay nothing for flexibility; a minority, with high valuations, would pay a great deal. Chapter twelve returns to hours, which turn out to be at the heart of the gender gap.
Theory: In 1957 Gary Becker gave discrimination an economic model. Suppose some employers dislike hiring a minority group. An employer with a taste for discrimination d behaves as if a minority worker cost the wage times one plus d. Line up the Island's employers from the least prejudiced to the most: here, only 5 percent have no prejudice at all. Minority workers, an eighth of the labour force, are hired first by the least prejudiced employers, until all have jobs. The market wage gap is set by the last employer needed to hire them: the marginal employer's taste, here 1.3 percent. The most prejudiced employers simply hire no minority workers at all.

Becker's model makes a striking prediction. Raise the share of employers with no prejudice, and the market gap shrinks, reaching zero once the unprejudiced alone can hire every minority worker. The average employer's tastes do not matter; the marginal employer's do. Prejudice also costs the prejudiced: they pay more for the same work, so competition should let fair employers grow and push the others out. Discrimination can persist if the taste belongs to customers or co-workers, whom firms must please, or if employers have the wage-setting power of Part thirty-eight, which lets them pay groups differently without losing them.

A second theory needs no prejudice at all. In 1972 Edmund Phelps imagined an employer who cannot see productivity, only a noisy signal, such as a test score or an interview, and pays what the worker is expected to produce. The best guess shrinks the score towards the group's average, by more when the score is noisier. For a group whose scores the employer reads precisely, pay follows the score closely. For a group whose scores are noisier to this employer, perhaps because the interviewers share less background with them, pay is flatter. The two groups have the same average ability, yet a high scorer from the second group is paid less: equal scores, unequal pay, from statistics alone. Kenneth Arrow added the sting: if workers from a group expect their skills to be read poorly, investing in skills pays them less, so they may invest less, and the employer's belief comes true.
Measured: Return to the résumés, the cleanest kind of evidence: the employer sees everything about the candidate except a randomly assigned name, so any difference in call-backs is caused by the name. The gap appears in both cities, for women's names and men's names alike. And the researchers made some résumés stronger than others: more experience, honours, skills. A better résumé raised call-backs by 2.3 percentage points for White names, but only 0.5 for African-American names. Investing in a stronger résumé paid less for the group discriminated against, Arrow's mechanism in the data.

There are two kinds of field experiment. In an audit study, trained pairs of applicants, alike except in race or sex, apply in person: realistic, but the actors know what is being tested. In a correspondence study, like the résumés, only paper is sent: cleaner, but it sees only the first step of hiring. In 2017 Lincoln Quillian, Devah Pager and colleagues combined the American field experiments run since 1989: White applicants received on average 36 percent more call-backs than African Americans, with no decline over twenty-five years. And when American orchestras began auditioning players behind a screen, Claudia Goldin and Cecilia Rouse found that women became more likely to advance and be hired, though, as they note, some of their estimates are imprecise.

Most data are not experiments. The standard tool for them is the Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition, from 1973: split a pay gap into a part explained by differences in measured characteristics and a part that remains. In a 1978 sample from the Current Population Survey, men's log wages exceeded women's by 0.35; schooling, experience, union membership and the rest explain only 0.03 of it. By 1985 the gap was 0.23, and the measured characteristics explain none of it. But the unexplained part is not a measure of discrimination. It also contains everything not measured: actual rather than potential experience, hours, the field of study. And some controls, such as occupation, may themselves be shaped by discrimination, so adding them hides it. A decomposition describes; only a design like the résumés can say what causes what.
Gender: In 1979 the median woman working full time in America earned 62 percent of the median man's weekly pay. Over the next two decades the gap closed fast, as women's schooling caught up and then overtook men's, and women entered professions they had been kept out of: by 2000 the ratio was 77 percent. Since then it has crept up, to 82 percent in 2025. The question is what is left.

Claudia Goldin, who received the Nobel prize for this work in 2023, argued that the last chapter is about time. In many jobs, pay rises in proportion to hours. In others, long hours, and hours at particular times, the evening meeting, the client call at night, are rewarded more than in proportion, because one person who is always available is worth more than two who share the work. Whoever in a couple takes the flexible job, usually the mother, earns less per hour. Pharmacy, she showed, became a flexible profession, with a small gender gap; law and finance did not.

When does the gap open? In 2019 Henrik Kleven, Camille Landais and Jakob Egholt Søgaard followed Danish parents through the government's records, year by year around the birth of their first child, comparing them with their own earlier selves and with people of the same age who had a child at a different time. On the Island, the same design: fathers' earnings barely move when the child arrives. Mothers' fall by 26 percent in the first year, and never recover: ten years later they are about 20 percent below where they would have been. The Island's truth is planted, and the design recovers it. In Denmark the long-run penalty is about 20 percent, through fewer hours, less work and lower pay per hour, and the share of the remaining gender gap caused by children rose from about 40 percent in 1980 to about 80 percent by 2013.

That makes it one of the series' facts. In the data, the gender gap in earnings opens at the birth of the first child. The theory is about hours, flexibility, and who in a couple takes the flexible job. And Agora's event study recovers a planted penalty of about the size the Danish records show.
Practice: Chapter fourteen. In practice: pay audits and workforce plans.

Who uses this? Pay-equity analysts, inside firms and for regulators, run the regressions of chapter eleven on a firm's own payroll, comparing like with like. Workforce planners ask which tasks machines will take and whom to retrain. Compensation teams set pay bands from market surveys. And labour economists in government bring discrimination cases, run the earnings statistics this part used, and advise on policy.

A pay audit is the decomposition of chapter eleven, done on one employer. Take the payroll; compare people in the same job family, level and location; measure what gap remains; and either explain it or fix it. The trap is the same as before: if women are promoted more slowly, controlling for level hides exactly the discrimination the audit is meant to find.

Called it? In 1983 Wassily Leontief, who won the Nobel prize for input-output analysis, told a symposium that the role of humans as the most important factor of production was bound to diminish, as the role of horses in farming had been diminished and then eliminated by tractors. Forty years on, a larger share of Americans in their prime work than in 1983: 73.7 percent then, 80.7 percent in 2025. But labour's share of business income has fallen by about 12 percent, and the middle of the wage distribution has hollowed out. The verdict: too early to say. Horses, unlike people, could not move to new tasks; whether people always can is exactly what artificial intelligence will test.
